item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.note1: Measures how far away something is without going there. Sight the same mark from two places and the triangle tells you the distance.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.note2: Telescope + vernier caliper (vernier scale) + 2 bronze + 2 sticks. Hold right-click to look, release to read the direction. 1) sight a mark and release (station A) -> 2) walk at least 3 m sideways, sight the same mark and release (station B) -> the base and two angles give the distance. Sneak + right-click clears station A.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.note3: In 1615 the Dutchman Snellius measured the distance between towns with a chain of triangles (triangulation). Measure one base line carefully and angles alone do the rest of the country. In the 18th century the theodolite combined a telescope with graduated circles.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.note4: Sine rule: with base c and end angles alpha and beta, distance from B = c sin(alpha) / sin(alpha + beta). The thinner the triangle (far target, short base), the more a small angle error grows. Ino Tadataka (1800-1821) mapped Japan by combining walked traverses with sightings of mountain peaks from many places.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.placeh: Approximation: the base length is taken directly as the distance between the two stations (really it was measured on the ground with chains or rods). No link to map items yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.statio: 📐 Station A recorded: bearing %s°. Walk sideways and sight the same mark
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.short_: The base is only %s m. Move at least %s m away first
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.no_cro: The two sight lines do not cross ahead. Did you sight the same mark? (station A kept)
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.result: 📐 Base %s m, angle A %s°, angle B %s° -> %s m from here to the target (at %s, %s)
item.semiconductor-lab.theodolite.real: The block you sighted is really %s m away (off by %s m)
A machine that holds a room's temperature and humidity steady. Precise machines grow and shrink with temperature, so air conditioning matters.

Refrigerating machine + motor + copper cable + 6 iron. Uses 2 kW the whole time it runs. Within 8 blocks the temperature swing drops from +-3 C to +-0.1 C, cutting the mask aligner's thermal overlay error (the stage growing and shrinking) from 3.3 um to 0.1 um.

In 1902 the American Carrier built air conditioning that held temperature and humidity for a printing plant where damp paper stretched and colors misregistered. Air conditioning was born for paper, not people.
Steel grows about 11 um per metre per degree, which is why lengths are measured in rooms held at the standard 20 C (CIPM 1931). Today's lithography rooms hold temperature to a hundredth of a degree.
Approximation: the temperature swings (+-3 C, +-0.1 C) and range (8 blocks) are game values. Humidity control is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_fiber.note1: Glass melted and drawn out into thin threads.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_fiber.note2: 4 from 2 soda-lime glass + platinum bushing (returned). 7 + 2 iron make a HEPA filter.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_fiber.note3: Molten glass pulled through small holes becomes threads finer than a hair. Mass production began in the 1930s for insulation, filters and reinforced plastics.
item.semiconductor-lab.glass_fiber.note4: Thin glass bends without breaking easily. Optical fibre is also a thin thread of very pure silica glass.
item.semiconductor-lab.hepa_filter.note1: A filter that removes almost all the tiny dust in the air.
item.semiconductor-lab.hepa_filter.note2: 7 glass fibre + 2 iron. Goes in the air conditioner's filter slot and becomes the air inlet of a cleanroom [12-14].
item.semiconductor-lab.hepa_filter.note3: Developed in the 1940s in the Manhattan Project to catch radioactive dust. It removes at least 99.97% of 0.3 um particles.
item.semiconductor-lab.hepa_filter.note4: Large particles hit the fibres and tiny ones wander into them (Brownian motion). Mid-sized particles around 0.3 um are the hardest to catch, so performance is rated at that size.
item.semiconductor-lab.hepa_filter.place: Approximation: real HEPA media is pleated ultra-fine borosilicate glass fibre (soda-lime glass fibre here).
A platinum plate with many tiny holes. Molten glass pulled through it becomes threads.
3 platinum. With 2 soda-lime glass it makes 4 glass fibre (the bushing returns).
In the 1930s Owens-Corning and others began mass-producing glass fibre by pulling molten glass through tiny holes in platinum plates.
Platinum neither dissolves in glass above 1000 C nor corrodes. Platinum-rhodium bushings are still used today.
Approximation: the heat to melt the glass is skipped (drawn in the crafting grid).
block.semiconductor-lab.hepa_ceiling.not: A ceiling outlet that sends clean air from the top down.

HEPA filter + 2 iron -> 2. Lay them across the ceiling of an enclosed room and run an air conditioner with a HEPA filter inside to make a cleanroom. With 80% or more of the ceiling it is class 100, with 25% class 1000. Wafers exposed by a mask aligner inside stay cleaner (outside: dirt +2).
In 1962 Whitfield at Sandia Laboratories devised the laminar-flow cleanroom, sending air one way from a ceiling of HEPA filters to the floor to sweep dust away, cutting room dust hundreds of times.

Cleanroom class counts particles of 0.5 um or larger per cubic foot of air (class 100 = at most 100; US Federal Standard 209, 1963). Today's fabs are thousands of times cleaner than an operating room. People are the biggest source of dust, so workers wear full-body cleanroom suits.
block.semiconductor-lab.hepa_ceiling.pla: Approximation: the class thresholds (80% and 25% of the ceiling) are game values. A room is at most 512 air blocks.
block.semiconductor-lab.roman_concrete.n: Concrete of lime and volcanic ash that lasts 2000 years.
Wet mix (slaked lime + 2 tuff + 2 gravel -> 4) sets when it touches water. Mine with a pickaxe.

Slaked lime Ca(OH)2 reacts in water with the silicon and aluminium of volcanic ash (pozzolana) to form insoluble stony compounds (calcium silicate hydrates and others) - the pozzolanic reaction. So it sets even underwater.

The dome of Rome's Pantheon (about AD 128) is unreinforced concrete and still among the largest of its kind. Harbour walls in the sea are said to have grown stronger from crystals formed with seawater ⚠️.
block.semiconductor-lab.roman_concrete.p: Approximation: vanilla tuff stands in for volcanic ash (pozzolana) (decision). It sets instantly (real concrete gains strength over days).
block.semiconductor-lab.roman_concrete_m: Concrete that has not set yet. It sets when it touches water.
Slaked lime + 2 tuff + 2 gravel -> 4. It falls like sand when placed. Placed next to water (poured into water) it sets into Roman concrete.
With water the lime-ash reaction starts and it hardens (hydraulic). Ordinary lime plaster sets with CO2 from the air, so it will not set underwater.
Romans sank wooden forms into the sea and poured the mix into them to build harbour walls.
item.semiconductor-lab.cement_raw_meal.n: Powder of limestone and clay. Fired, it becomes the base of cement.
3 calcite (limestone) + clay -> 2. Fire in a blast furnace -> clinker.
About 80% limestone (CaCO3) and 20% clay (oxides of silicon, aluminium, iron). If the ratio drifts, it sets poorly.
Cement works are built next to limestone quarries.
item.semiconductor-lab.cement_raw_meal.p: Approximation: calcite stands in for limestone (whose main mineral is calcite).
item.semiconductor-lab.cement_clinker.no: Grey, half-melted lumps from the kiln. Ground, they become cement.
Fire raw meal in a blast furnace. 2 + gypsum -> 4 Portland cement.
At about 1450 °C, lime and clay react to calcium silicates (alite Ca3SiO5, belite Ca2SiO4) and others, which set by reacting with water (hydration).
From the 1880s it was fired in long, slowly turning cylinders (rotary kilns). Cement-making is said to release about 8% of the world's CO2 (from the limestone and from fuel) ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.portland_cement.n: A grey powder. With water, sand and gravel it becomes concrete.
2 clinker + gypsum -> 4. + 4 sand + 4 gravel -> 8 grey concrete powder (sets when it touches water).
A little gypsum is added so it does not set the instant water goes in. Cement sets by reacting with water (not by drying), so it even sets underwater.
Joseph Aspdin in England patented it in 1824. Its set colour resembled Portland stone, hence the name.
block.semiconductor-lab.reinforced_concr: Concrete with steel bars inside. Very strong.
8 grey concrete + steel (rebar) -> 8. More than ten times as blast-resistant as ordinary concrete.

Concrete is strong in compression but very weak in tension; steel is strong in tension. They expand with heat at almost the same rate, so they do not crack apart in heat and cold, and concrete's alkali keeps the steel from rusting.
In 1867 the French gardener Joseph Monier patented flowerpots with iron mesh inside. Most of today's buildings, bridges and dams use this pairing.
Approximation: strength is shown only as blast resistance (really tensile and bending strength).
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_bath.note1: A shallow tub of molten tin. Glass floats on it to become sheet.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_bath.note2: 5 tin + 4 refractory brick. Returned after crafting. 6 soda-lime glass + this -> 16 glass panes.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_bath.note3: Molten glass poured onto molten tin (about 1000 °C) floats, since it is lighter, and gravity and surface tension spread it into a perfectly flat sheet about 6 mm thick. The bottom touches tin and the top is fire-polished, so both come out mirror-flat. Nitrogen and hydrogen gas cover it so the tin does not oxidize.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_bath.note4: Alastair Pilkington in England announced the float process in 1959. Before that, sheet glass had to be ground and polished on both sides. Most window glass and phone-screen glass today is made this way.
item.semiconductor-lab.tin_bath.placehol: Approximation: the nitrogen-hydrogen cover and annealing are omitted. The tin is not used up.
block.semiconductor-lab.steel_beam.note1: A steel beam or column for the frames of tall buildings and bridges.
block.semiconductor-lab.steel_beam.note2: 7 steel -> 6. Like a log, it becomes a vertical column or a horizontal beam depending on how you place it.
block.semiconductor-lab.steel_beam.note3: The H-shaped section puts the material in the top and bottom flanges, making the beam stiff in bending for its weight. Steel is strong in both tension and compression, so a light frame can carry a tall building.
block.semiconductor-lab.steel_beam.note4: The Iron Bridge in England (1779) was the first big cast-iron bridge. Chicago's Home Insurance Building (1885) is counted among the first steel-framed skyscrapers ⚠️. The Eiffel Tower (wrought iron, 1889) changes height by more than ten centimetres between summer and winter (thermal expansion).
block.semiconductor-lab.steel_beam.place: Approximation: only the look and orientation; the building's loads are not calculated.
block.semiconductor-lab.macadam.note1: A road of packed broken stone. You walk a little faster.
block.semiconductor-lab.macadam.note2: 2 cobblestone + 2 gravel -> 4. Walking speed x1.15. + coal tar -> tar macadam.
block.semiconductor-lab.macadam.note3: Layers of angular broken stone rolled with a heavy roller lock together and do not turn to mud in rain; the crown of the road sheds water.
block.semiconductor-lab.macadam.note4: John Loudon McAdam of Scotland spread the method around 1820. Before that, roads turned to mud in rain and coaches could not move.
block.semiconductor-lab.macadam.placehol: Approximation: layer thickness and rolling are omitted.
block.semiconductor-lab.tarmac.note1: A black road of broken stone bound with coal tar. You walk even faster.
block.semiconductor-lab.tarmac.note2: 4 macadam + coal tar -> 4. Walking speed x1.3.
block.semiconductor-lab.tarmac.note3: Tar fills the gaps and glues the stones, keeping water out so car tyres do not pluck the stones loose.
block.semiconductor-lab.tarmac.note4: In 1902 Edgar Hooley in England noticed a stretch of road where tar had spilled was hard and dust-free, and patented 'tarmac' (tar + macadam). Today's asphalt comes from petroleum (not in this mod).
block.semiconductor-lab.tarmac.placehold: Approximation: the speed factor is a game value.
Just connect power (copper cable). Nearby temperature swings shrink, so precision machines drift less. Add a HEPA filter for clean-room air.
block.semiconductor-lab.cast_iron_pipe.n: An iron pipe that carries water far away. Let it touch a water source block and run it to a tap.
3 pig iron -> 3 pipes. Pipes, sand filters and chlorinators connect when they touch (up to 256).
Roman aqueducts carried mountain water to the city down gentle slopes in stone channels and lead pipes. Cast iron pipes stand the water pressure inside and spread under cities in the 19th century.
From the 1810s London replaced its wooden mains with cast iron. Roman aqueducts (from the Aqua Appia, 312 BC) fell only tens of centimetres per kilometre ⚠️.
block.semiconductor-lab.cast_iron_pipe.p: Approximation: flow rate, amount and pressure are not calculated (only whether it is connected).
block.semiconductor-lab.sand_filter.note: A tank that passes water slowly through sand to remove murk and germs. Put it in the water main.
3 sand + 3 gravel + a cast iron pipe -> 1. Connected to the pipes, the tap gives filtered water.
Microbes living in the slimy layer on top of the sand (the biofilm) eat germs in the water - it is not just sieving.
In 1829 James Simpson of the Chelsea Waterworks began slow sand filtration for a city supply. In Hamburg's 1892 cholera, neighbouring Altona, which filtered its water, had far fewer cases ⚠️.
block.semiconductor-lab.sand_filter.plac: Approximation: the time for the biofilm to grow and cleaning when it clogs are skipped.
block.semiconductor-lab.water_tap.note1: An outlet for piped water. Right-click with an empty glass bottle.
block.semiconductor-lab.water_tap.note2: Cast iron pipe + copper ingot -> 1. No water comes unless the pipes touch a water source.
block.semiconductor-lab.water_tap.note3: What comes out depends on what is in the line: nothing = murky water, a sand filter = filtered water, plus a chlorinator = disinfected water.
block.semiconductor-lab.water_tap.note4: In old cities wells and rivers mixed with sewage and cholera and typhoid spread. Clean piped water is said to have saved more lives than medicines ⚠️.
block.semiconductor-lab.chlorinator.note: A device that dissolves a tiny amount of chlorine in the supply to kill germs.
7 iron + cast iron pipe -> 1. Right-click with a chlorine cylinder (yellow) for 16 doses. Each bottle drawn at the tap uses one.
Chlorine breaks the germs' membranes. It goes after the sand filter: in murky water germs hide in the particles.
In 1908 Jersey City, USA, became the first water supply chlorinated continuously. The 'pool smell' is that chlorine (and what it forms with sweat).
block.semiconductor-lab.chlorinator.plac: Approximation: chlorine concentration and residual are not calculated (doses only).
item.semiconductor-lab.murky_water.note1: Unfiltered river or pond water. Drinking it upsets your stomach (Hunger).
item.semiconductor-lab.murky_water.note2: Comes from a tap whose pipes have no sand filter.
item.semiconductor-lab.murky_water.note3: It may carry germs too small to see (cholera, typhoid). Boiling, or filtering then chlorinating, makes it safe.
item.semiconductor-lab.murky_water.note4: In 1854 John Snow mapped London's cholera cases and traced them to the Broad Street pump ([13-07]).
item.semiconductor-lab.filtered_water.no: Water filtered through sand. Clear, but sometimes it still upsets your stomach.
From a tap with a sand filter in the line. About 1 in 4 gives a short Hunger effect.
Sand filtration removes most germs, but not all - chlorine finishes the job.
Filtration plus chlorination cut typhoid deaths sharply in early 20th-century American cities ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.chlorinated_water: Water filtered through sand and disinfected with chlorine. Nothing happens when you drink it - safe water.
From a tap with a sand filter and a loaded chlorinator in the line.
Tap water today keeps a little chlorine all the way to the tap so germs do not grow in the pipes.
Japan's Waterworks Act requires a small chlorine residual at the tap ⚠️.
message.semiconductor-lab.water_tap.dry: No water. Check that the pipes touch a water source block
message.semiconductor-lab.water_tap.safe: Disinfected water came out (a faint smell of chlorine)
message.semiconductor-lab.chlorinator.le: Chlorine leaked while changing the cylinder! You feel sick (even a little is dangerous to breathe)
block.semiconductor-lab.water_tap.howto: Run cast iron pipes from a water source (pond, river) to the tap and right-click with an empty glass bottle. A sand filter, then a chlorinator, in the line give filtered and disinfected water.
block.semiconductor-lab.cesspit.note1: A pit that collects a household's dirty water. Near a water intake it spoils the water.
block.semiconductor-lab.cesspit.note2: 7 cobblestone + dirt -> 1. Within 6 blocks of the intake (the water the pipes touch), and not drained far away by sewer pipes, it makes tap water one step worse.
block.semiconductor-lab.cesspit.note3: Filth seeps through the ground into nearby wells and rivers. That is why sewage is carried far out of town by sewer pipes.
block.semiconductor-lab.cesspit.note4: In 1854 a cesspit right next to London's Broad Street well leaked cholera germs into it. John Snow found the well with a map ([13-07]).
block.semiconductor-lab.cesspit.placehol: Approximation: seepage is approximated as 'within 6 blocks'.
block.semiconductor-lab.sewer_pipe.note1: A big concrete pipe that carries sewage out of town.
block.semiconductor-lab.sewer_pipe.note2: 4 gray concrete -> 4. Run pipes from the cesspit more than 16 blocks away and the filth is carried off, so the tap water stays clean.
block.semiconductor-lab.sewer_pipe.note3: Sewers slope gently down to carry waste downstream or to a treatment works. Separating drinking water from sewage is the basis of city hygiene.
block.semiconductor-lab.sewer_pipe.note4: In the summer of 1858 the 'Great Stink' of the Thames stopped Parliament, and Joseph Bazalgette's sewer network (1860s, using huge amounts of concrete) followed ⚠️.
block.semiconductor-lab.sewer_pipe.place: Approximation: slope and flow are not calculated (only whether it connects far enough).
